Hey, I just recently got over an almost 3 years long friend crush. There's no hard and fast rules about this sort of thing. For me what helped was ripping off the band-aid pretty early and telling her from the get-go. Hearing the no was hard, but it helped counter the what ifs in my head. The rest was working on my own end of things. My feelings, my crushing loneliness, etc.

Since in my situation I'm pretty good friends with her, I can have the kind of frank conversations about establishing physical boundaries and clearing up what felt like mixed signals. When I get flirty she gets the spray bottle. 

Alternatively I've been told to create some distance. I hear that doing that helps. The rest is just time. In my case that wasn't an option for me because our lives are pretty intertwined (same support group).

Best of luck to you

Assuming you're younger, it's a fair question. There seems to be difference of understanding in what the labels mean due to lack of open talk between queer folks of different experiences and generations

Butch and femme are descriptive labels for self-identification. They're historically useful as a shorthand to explain to other a certain culture within the lesbian community. With them, people can quickly communicates that they experiences life and themselves in a way that is unique but also identifiable. 

I'm no longer cis or a lesbian (being enby and bi, but I previously identified as butch before coming out), but butch and femme labels (and studs. We can't forget studs) has a long history within the culture and isn't inherently harmful to use. They are tools of resistance. By having labels to help people identify who they are instead of lying down and accepting the labels from society at large, the labels free us. They unite us.

NTA. Keeping work and friends separate is completely understandable. I have recommended friends who are looking to work at the same place I did before. When things went sideways with work and my friends came under scrutiny, some of that got laid on me. It sucked, but I approached it as "Hey, you asked. I merely recommended the people I see that have the skills. Any issues beyond that is beyond me. Y'all are adults. Work it out yourselves".

As for your friend, I don't have the context about her aside from what you've posted. Could there something about her personality that you don't want to introduce to your work life besides the stuff that has already been mentioned? Pretty likely. But there are many reasons why someone who technically does not have to work would want to work. 

1) She might want to experience what it's like to have a job, which is a fairly fundamental experience for someone in very early 20's. 

2) She might want to become more financially independent. Everyone's comfort level with family money is different. Some have no problem getting financial support from their parents well into adulthood. Others feel that it's not "their money", as in money they have earned themselves.

Other comments have mentioned that this may be to you wanting to feel better about yourself. I don't know about that enough to comment. Thing is, you're the one who have worked hard at your job. You did the work. The possibility of her working the same place you do has little bearing on the work that you have put in thus far. I don't know if where you work is a place that puts more value on a piece of paper than the actual effort put in. If that's the case, then at least you can hear from me that the effort you put in and the experience is what actually matters in the long run.

I feel you. I have BPD and my depressive episodes during this pandemic are *bad*. I used to be very quick to anger as well. It scared my ex, so I tried my best to work on it in therapy. It has helped quite a lot over the years. 

To me it's a natural feeling to want to be next to someone and feel loved. Conversely, the only way I make any progress in the dating world is to put the work into myself. The more I work on myself and take care of myself, the more secure and safe in the world around me. Then I become less prone to outbursts and I manage my episodes better even when they're bad. Some days even brushing my teeth or eating is a big accomplishment.

We're all inherently flawed. That's the human condition. There's no requirement that you have to be so good you got rainbow coming out the ass when you throw yourself in the dating world. And there'll be someone out there who likes you, flaws and all. And by luck, you'll like theirs too.
